editorNote: A holiday desk of movie games, home-computer standards and household control.
morningLine: The Commodore 64 has a new line of work: catching ghosts.

lead.headline: Ghostbusters turns the Commodore 64 into a movie franchise
lead.dek: December’s game reviews put a familiar movie business on the home computer.
body: Activision’s Ghostbusters puts the Commodore 64 owner in charge of a ghost-catching franchise. Computer Gaming World’s December roundup finds the movie license well executed, with a particular eye for the machine’s graphics and sound. It is a holiday-season review, not an announcement of a Christmas-week shipment.

The player begins with $2,000 in game capital and must buy a vehicle and ghost-catching hardware. That sum belongs to the simulation’s business ledger, not to a shop’s price tag. The premise makes the film’s comic enterprise into something the player can manage at the keyboard.

The magazine says the program “showcases the graphics and sound capabilities of the C-64” and judges that it should appeal to people who saw the movie. The familiar title thus arrives with a machine-specific attraction: the home computer supplies the sound and moving picture as well as the decisions.

Ghostbusters shares the December roundup with Zenji, Park Patrol, Space Shuttle and Zone Ranger. The breadth of that shelf matters as much as the license: buyers can choose a pathway puzzle, an arcade challenge or a spacecraft alongside the recognizable cinema name. No verified sales total or exact Christmas-week release date accompanies this review.

stories.headline: MSX promises a common language for incompatible home computers
body: Home computers have made a habit of speaking incompatible languages. COMPUTE!’s December report by Tom R. Halfhill and Selby Bateman offers MSX as a possible escape: conforming cartridges, disks, tapes and peripherals could work across machines bearing different manufacturers’ names.

The common specification uses a Zilog Z80A processor, TI 9918A video, 16 colors, 32 sprites and three-channel sound. The report describes 32K ROM and 16K to 64K RAM. Sony, Yamaha, Panasonic, Sanyo, JVC and Hitachi appear in a scheme that makes the software library less dependent on the badge on the case.

The authors report more than 265,000 units sold by midsummer after the Japanese debut in November 1983. Their expected January Las Vegas introduction and low-end American prices around $200 or less remain prospects, not current offers. MSX-DOS disk-format compatibility should not be mistaken for the ability to run IBM programs.

stories.headline: A Commodore can switch the lights and watch the windows
body: A computer can do household work without becoming a robot. Sharon Darling’s December COMPUTE! feature describes Genesis controllers for the VIC-20 and Commodore 64, with timed lighting and appliance schedules passed through BSR-type remote switches.

The VIController is quoted at $69.95 with disk software; COMsense costs another $69.95. Used with magnetic reed switches, the sensing accessory can signal an opened window or door. Plug-in modules and sensors remain part of the installation, not free extras hidden inside the controller price.

James Coffron estimates around $200 for a simple Commodore-based control setup. The feature ranges further into temperature, soil moisture and humidity sensing, but its predictions of energy savings and future computer-equipped houses are expectations, not measured results.

stories.headline: Year-end editors still choose the under-$200 Commodore 64
body: David H. Ahl’s December Creative Computing buying guide puts the Commodore 64 first in the under-$500 home-computer category. Thirteen editors weigh software, support, distribution and usability alongside specifications; the reported street price is generally below $200 for the computer itself.

The verdict is no blank cheque. Ahl records complaints about the slow disk drive, cursor keys, nonstandard interfaces and manufacturer support. The Plus/4’s integrated applications do not erase its lack of sprites or its incompatibility with much of the established C-64 library.

The notebook counter offers another calculation. Radio Shack’s Model 100 takes the under-$1,000 category at $599 for 8K or $799 for 24K, helped by its built-in modem and store network. The guide’s category awards should not be read as a single winner for every buyer.

softwareList.name: Logo for the 64
softwareList.detail: Andrew Keith’s December COMPUTE! review, p. 138: Terrapin-developed Commodore Logo supports turtle graphics, sprites, sound and list processing; includes manual/tutorial and utilities/demo disk. Reported range $50–$80, with some sales as low as $35.

worldAnchor.headline: Moscow chooses a veteran defense minister after Ustinov’s death
worldAnchor.summary: December 24 reporting describes Marshal Sergei Sokolov replacing Dmitri Ustinov as Soviet defense minister. The veteran appointment signals continuity while the question of leadership after Chernenko remains unsettled.

bbsNote.headline: An Apple modem bundle offers a doorway to The Source
bbsNote.summary: December COMPUTE! carries Zoom Telephonics’ NETWORKER modem starter-set advertisement; the Source offer explicitly expires December 31, 1984.

posts.platform: Apple II / II+ / IIe; The Source
posts.text: Period-ad synopsis, not a recovered BBS post: 300-baud modem card, menu-driven communications software and a subscription to The Source are bundled. No price or hourly service charge is stated in the inspected ad; do not invent one.
Period buying-guide synopsis, not a BBS post: Ahl names the built-in modem as one reason the Model 100 beats the NEC PC-8201 in the under-$1,000 notebook category.

curiosity.headline: A joystick paint program dangles a $10,000 prize
curiosity.summary: Activision advertises The Designer’s Pencil as a C-64 way to create graphics and accompanying music, and invites users into a $10,000 contest.
curiosity.detail: The December COMPUTE! ad credits Garry Kitchen and says contest details are in specially marked packages. The $10,000 is the advertised contest amount, not a verified award paid that week; no deadline or winners were inspected.

periodAd.headline: NETWORKER opens a line to The Source
periodAd.summary: Zoom Telephonics advertises an Apple II-family 300-baud modem card, communications software and a subscription to The Source. The advertised Source offer expires December 31, 1984; no price or hourly service charge is quoted here.
periodAd.tagline: A modem starter set for the Apple desk.

market.headline: A software library adds weight to the price tag
market.summary: The C-64’s established library supports its buying-guide verdict; MSX proposes sharing software between brands. Hardware price alone cannot settle the cost of choosing a home-computer system.
